title: Online Safety
summary: Being safe, responsible and respectful online: e-safety, protecting your personal information and thinking before you share.
learn: Which personal information is risky to share
Asking for consent before posting photos of others
Staying safe on social media, gaming and messaging
intro: How to stay safe and be responsible online: protecting personal information, safe gaming and downloading, social networks, cyberbullying, grooming, your digital footprint, what to do if you are worried, and the team e-safety video project.

pages.spec: Explain what e-safety is and why your privacy matters
pages.summary: E-safety is the safe and responsible use of technology: the internet, texts, gaming, email and smart devices. It is as much about how you behave as about security. Moving to secondary school, you become a more independent internet user, so knowing how to stay safe matters.

blocks.text: **[[E-safety]]** (or online safety) is the **safe, responsible and ethical** use of technology. This includes the internet, and other ways of communicating using electronic media: text messages, messaging apps, online gaming, email and smart connected devices.
E-safety isn't just the "common sense" stuff. In practice, e-safety is **as much about behaviour as it is about electronic security**: how you treat others, what you share and who you trust.
Why is your privacy important?

Have you ever had something private or secret about you get out? Online, it can spread much faster and much further. **[[Privacy]]** means keeping control of your personal information and who can see it.

head: Fact
What it tells us
rows: Nearly **1 in 3** 11–13 year olds have broadcast themselves live on the internet
Live streaming is common, and once it's out it can be recorded by anyone watching.
**81%** of 8–17 year olds say they know when and how to ask permission to post something about someone else
Most young people know they should ask first…
**52%** say someone they know shared a photo or video of them without asking
…but over half have had their own photo shared without permission.
**47%** of young people think it's important to 'fit in' online
Pressure to fit in can push people to share more than they should.
blocks.caption: Young people online: the facts

blocks.text: Becoming a good online citizen

As you move to secondary school you become a more independent and confident internet user with more varied habits. The internet can be hugely positive, but there are dangers if we use it wrongly. That's why we keep talking about online safety: so you become a good **[[online citizen]]**.

blocks.title: Worked example: why ask before posting a photo of a friend?
blocks.context: 52% of 8–17 year olds say someone shared a photo or video of them without asking. Why is asking for consent before posting photos of others an important part of good online behaviour?
steps: It is their image: they have a right to decide who sees it.
They might be embarrassed or upset by it, which could even become cyberbullying.
It could reveal personal information, like their school uniform or location.
Once posted, it can be copied and shared and can't be taken back.
blocks.answer: Always ask first, because you can't undo a post, and it's respectful.

blocks.title: Key points
items: E-safety = the safe and responsible use of technology.
It covers the internet, texts, gaming, email and smart devices.
E-safety is as much about behaviour as electronic security.
Always ask before posting a photo or video of someone else.

check.q: What is e-safety?
o: The safe and responsible use of technology
check.why: E-safety is safe and responsible technology use.

check.q: E-safety is as much about ______ as it is about electronic security.
check.why: How you behave online matters as much as security.

check.q: What percentage of 8–17 year olds said someone shared a photo or video of them without asking?
check.why: 52% reported this.

check.q: Which of these does e-safety cover?
o: The internet, texts, gaming and email
check.why: It covers all electronic communication.

practice.q: Define **e-safety**.
practice.a: The safe and responsible use of technology (1), including the internet and other electronic communication such as texts, gaming and email (1).

practice.q: Explain why you should ask permission before posting a photo of a friend online.
practice.a: It's their image and they have a right to choose / they might be upset or embarrassed (1); once posted it can be copied and shared and can't be taken back (1).

pages.spec: Identify personal information and judge how risky it is to share online
pages.summary: Personal information such as your home address, phone number, email, date of birth, school and photos should be kept private. Some details are high risk because they let strangers find or contact you; others, like your favourite game genre, are low risk.

blocks.text: **[[Personal information]]** is information that could identify you, or help someone find or contact you. The golden rule: **KEEP IT PRIVATE**, and that includes online.
Which are personal information?

head: Item
Personal information to keep private?
rows: Yes: it helps strangers target you
Can be: they often reveal where you are or what you're doing
Lower risk on its own, but adds to a picture of who you are
Lower risk, but tells people how public your account is
blocks.caption: Is it personal information?

blocks.text: How risky is it to share?

head: Data item
Risk
Why it is a risk if exposed online
rows: Lets strangers find your exact home.
The uniform and badge show which school you go to, so someone could find you there.
Strangers can contact you directly, privately, at any time, away from the platform's safety tools.
Doesn't identify or locate you, though groomers can use shared interests to build trust.
Date of birth and full name
Can be used to steal your identity, guess passwords and find you on other sites.
[[Geotagging]] shows exactly where you are right now, so someone could come and find you.
blocks.caption: Personal data risk table (completed)

blocks.text: Before you share anything, ask: *Could a stranger use this to find me, contact me or pretend to be me?* If yes, keep it private.
Small pieces of low-risk information add up. Your first name + your football club + a photo outside your house can be pieced together to find you.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Personal information can identify you, locate you or let someone contact you.
Keep your address, phone number, email, date of birth, full name, school and photos private.
School uniform photos and geotagged posts are high risk.
Small, low-risk details can add up to a full picture of you.

diagram.title: High or low risk?
diagram.caption: Decide, then click to check.
head: Data item
Risk
Reason
rows: Date of birth and full name
Shows where you are right now

check.q: Which of these is the highest risk to post online?
check.why: Your address lets strangers find you.

check.q: Why is a photo in your school uniform risky?
o: It shows which school you go to
check.why: It tells people where to find you every weekday.

check.q: What is a geotagged status update?
o: A post with your exact location attached
check.why: Geotagging adds your location.

check.q: What should you do with personal information?
check.why: KEEP IT PRIVATE.

practice.q: List **four** examples of personal information that you should keep private online.
practice.a: Any four: home address (1); phone number (1); email address (1); date of birth (1); full name (1); school (1); photos (1); bank details (1).

practice.q: Explain why sharing a live geotagged status update is high risk.
practice.a: It shows your exact location in real time (1), so a stranger could find you / know your home is empty (1).

pages.spec: Make safe choices about photos, friends, posts and privacy settings
pages.summary: Photos posted online are there for ever. Only accept friends you know in real life, don't announce holidays or post personal details, use an avatar, and set your profile to private so only real friends can see it.

blocks.text: Becky's story (a video shown in class) is about a girl who shared too much online. These statements test what you'd do. Here are the answers.

blocks.title: True or false?
blocks.context: "It is OK to post a photo of yourself in your school uniform on social networking sites."
steps: If you put a photo on the internet, it's there **forever**. You can't fully delete it or take it back.
Your uniform shows where you go to school.
**Never** send photos to people you don't know, and never post pictures you wouldn't want your parents, teacher or grandparent to see.
Don't use your own photo as a profile picture. Use a cool graphic, called an **[[avatar]]**, instead.

blocks.title: True or false?
blocks.context: "It is OK to accept friends online even if you don't know them in person."
steps: Friends get access to more information about you, your other friends and your personal details.
The average person has around 55 real-life friends but over 200 online 'friends'.
Don't just add 'friends of friends': you have no idea who they really are.
Adults with bad intentions can pretend to be young people and try to contact children.

blocks.title: True or false?
blocks.context: "It is OK to post when I go on holiday."
steps: You've just told everyone your house is empty.
It wouldn't be nice to come home and find you'd been burgled.
Post your holiday photos **after** you get home.

blocks.title: True or false?
blocks.context: "It is OK to update my status with personal information such as my phone number."
steps: Your status could be seen by anyone, even 'friends of friends of friends'.
You wouldn't give your number to a stranger in the street, so why share it online?
You don't know what people will do with your personal information.

blocks.title: True or false?
blocks.context: "It is a good idea to keep my profile private so only close friends and family can see it."
steps: [[Privacy settings]] restrict who can see your posts and status updates.
This gives you more control, so only your real friends see what you post.
You can also block contact requests and only give access to people you actually know.

blocks.text: Think before you post

A funny or embarrassing photo of someone might seem harmless. But what happens when someone uses a photo like that to make **you** feel uncomfortable? **Never** post photos you wouldn't want your granny or your teacher to see. Employers often look up people's social media, and silly photos, even from when you were young and even ones you didn't post yourself, could affect whether you get a job.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Photos online are there forever; never send photos to strangers.
Use an avatar instead of your own photo.
Only accept friends you know in real life.
Don't post that you're on holiday or share your phone number.
Keep your profile private using privacy settings.

states.label: Public profile
points: Anyone can see your posts and photos
Friends of friends of friends can see your status
Your information can be copied by anyone

states.label: Private profile
points: Only approved friends see your posts
You choose who can tag you

check.q: What is an avatar?
o: A picture or character used instead of your real photo
check.why: An avatar represents you without showing your face.

check.q: Why shouldn't you post that you're on holiday while you're away?
o: People know your house is empty
check.why: Burglars could find out your home is empty.

check.q: Is it a good idea to keep your profile private?
o: Yes, so only real friends and family can see it
check.why: Privacy settings give you control.

check.q: Someone you don't know, but who is a 'friend of a friend', sends you a friend request. What should you do?
o: Decline: you don't know who they really are
check.why: Only accept people you know in real life.

practice.q: Give **three** pieces of advice about sharing photos online.
practice.a: Any three: photos online are there forever/can't be taken back (1); never send photos to people you don't know (1); don't post anything you wouldn't want parents/teachers to see (1); use an avatar as your profile picture (1); don't post photos in school uniform (1); ask before posting photos of others (1).

practice.q: Explain why you should only accept people you know in real life as online friends.
practice.a: Online friends gain access to your personal details/posts/friends (1); people online may not be who they say they are, e.g. adults pretending to be young people (1).

pages.spec: Describe the risks of online gaming and how to stay safe
pages.summary: Online gaming lets you play in real time with people worldwide. Risks include offensive chat, strangers, griefing and in-game purchases running up big bills. Stay safe by telling parents who you play with, reporting abuse, protecting personal details and controlling purchases.

blocks.text: **[[Online gaming]]** means you can play **in real time** with people across the world through an electronic device. **91%** of children are gamers. The average Fortnite player spends **6–10 hours a week** playing, and **68.8%** of Fortnite players have spent money on in-game purchases.
What you need to know

head: Risk
What it means
rows: Some games let you chat to anyone in the world, through headsets or text boxes, so you may come across offensive language and bullying.
Not everyone online is who they say they are. Gamers you meet online are strangers.
Games encourage you to buy extras like skins and currency. These have run up large bills without people realising.
Deliberately spoiling other players' games through harassment or cheating; sometimes used as a tactic to win. You could end up bullying or being bullied.
blocks.caption: Online gaming risks

blocks.text: Keeping safe while gaming

items: **Tell your parents** who you play with online and who you meet and talk to.
**Use appropriate language** in live chat, and learn how to **report** abusive chat and block anti-social players.
On a tablet or phone, use **airplane mode** to play offline games, so you can't make accidental purchases or connect with strangers.
**Don't share personal information.** Keep gaming friends in the game rather than adding them to your other social networks.
**Never agree to meet** someone you only know from a game.
Ask a parent to set up **purchase controls** (e.g. a password for buying) on your console.

blocks.title: Worked example: what should Ryan do?
blocks.context: Ryan, 12, is playing an online shooter. Another player, 'Pro_Gamer99', says he's 13, gives Ryan free V-Bucks and asks for his Snapchat so they can 'squad up' more.
steps: Free gifts and quickly moving to a private app are warning signs.
Ryan should not give his Snapchat or any personal details: keep game friends in the game.
He should tell a parent about the player, and block/report if he feels uncomfortable.
blocks.answer: Say no, keep chat in the game, tell a trusted adult.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Online gaming = real-time play with people worldwide; 91% of children game.
Risks: offensive chat, strangers, griefing and in-game purchases.
Tell parents who you play with, report abuse and protect personal details.
Use airplane mode or purchase controls to avoid surprise bills.

check.q: What is griefing?
check.why: Griefing is deliberately harassing or spoiling the game for others.

check.q: What percentage of Fortnite players have spent money on in-game purchases?
check.why: 68.8% have spent money in-game.

check.q: Why use airplane mode on a phone game?
o: To stop accidental purchases and contact with strangers
check.why: Offline means no purchases or chat.

check.q: A gaming friend asks to add you on Instagram. What's the safest choice?
o: Keep them as a friend in the game only
check.why: Keep gaming friends in the game.

practice.q: Describe **two** risks of online gaming.
practice.a: Any two: offensive language/bullying in chat (1); strangers who aren't who they say they are (1); in-game purchases running up large bills (1); griefing (1).

practice.q: Give **three** ways to stay safe when gaming online.
practice.a: Any three: tell parents who you play with (1); report/block abusive players (1); use airplane mode/purchase controls (1); don't share personal information (1); keep gaming friends in the game only (1); never meet someone from a game (1).

pages.spec: Describe the risks of downloading content, including malware, phishing, pharming and copyright
pages.summary: Downloading music, films and games is useful, but files from illegal or unknown sites can carry viruses, trojans, worms and spyware. Phishing and pharming trick you into giving away details, and illegal downloading breaks copyright law.

blocks.text: The internet lets you download video, music, games and other files on demand, which is a great benefit. But downloading can also expose you to **viruses** and **[[spyware]]**, and illegal downloading breaks the law.
Things to keep in mind

items: **Check what you are downloading.** The film and music industries monitor the internet for people downloading illegally.
Downloading from **illegal sites** also risks downloading viruses or spyware at the same time.
Malware can also arrive through **emails, pop-ups, shared files, USB drives** and connected devices.

blocks.text: Threats when downloading

head: Threat
What it is and what it does
rows: Harmful code that attaches to genuine programs, copies itself and corrupts or deletes files.
Malware disguised as something you want, like a free game mod or film, that secretly opens a 'back door' so attackers can get in.
Malware that spreads itself from computer to computer across a network, slowing everything down.
Secretly watch what you do and record your key presses to steal passwords and bank details.
Fake emails or messages pretending to be a real organisation (a bank, a school, a game company) to trick you into giving away details.
Secretly redirects you from a real website to a fake copy, to capture your login details.
Illegally downloading or sharing music, films or software, which breaks UK copyright law.
blocks.caption: Download dangers

blocks.text: **[[Malware]]** (malicious software) is the name for all of these harmful programs. They can do anything from taking control of your computer to slowing it down.

blocks.title: Worked example: spot the phishing
blocks.context: Aoife gets an email: *"Dear Customer, your Robux account will be DELETED in 24 hours! Click here and enter your password to keep it."*
steps: 'Dear Customer': a real company would use your name.
Urgent threat (24 hours): designed to panic you.
Asks for your password: real companies never ask for this by email.
The link probably goes to a fake site (pharming-style).
blocks.answer: It's phishing. Don't click; tell an adult and delete it.

blocks.text: Free versions of paid games and films are a favourite hiding place for trojans. If it looks too good to be true, it probably is.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Downloads from illegal or unknown sites can carry malware.
Malware includes viruses, trojans, worms and spyware.
Phishing uses fake messages; pharming uses fake websites.
Illegally downloading music, films or software breaks copyright law.

diagram.title: Match the threat
diagram.caption: Click to match each threat with its description.
pairs: Attaches to programs, copies itself and damages files
Disguised as something you want, but lets attackers in
Secretly records what you type to steal passwords
A fake email pretending to be your bank
Sends you to a fake copy of a real website

check.q: A free game mod secretly lets a hacker into your computer. What is it?
check.why: A trojan is disguised as something you want.

check.q: What is phishing?
o: A fake email or message pretending to be a real organisation
check.why: Phishing tricks you with fake messages.

check.q: What does spyware do?
o: Secretly records what you do to steal information
check.why: Spyware watches you to steal data.

check.q: Why is downloading films from illegal sites a problem?
o: It breaks copyright law and may carry malware
check.why: It's illegal and risky.

practice.q: Explain the difference between phishing and pharming.
practice.a: Phishing uses fake emails/messages pretending to be from a genuine organisation to trick you into giving details (1); pharming redirects you to a fake copy of a genuine website to capture your details (1).

practice.q: Give **two** risks of downloading content from illegal websites.
practice.a: You could download viruses/spyware/malware at the same time (1); you are breaking copyright law and could be caught, as industries monitor illegal downloading (1).

pages.spec: Describe the benefits and risks of social networking and apps, and the settings that keep you safe
pages.summary: Social networks let you chat, meet people with similar interests and share photos, but most have a minimum age of 13. Risks include location sharing, tags, information spreading and strangers. Manage privacy settings, tag approvals and location services.

blocks.text: **[[Social networking]]** sites are a huge favourite. They let you **stay in touch** with friends, **meet new people** with similar interests and **share photos and videos**. Used well, they're a great place to show your creativity.
Age limits

The **lower age limit** for most social networks is **13**. This includes Facebook, Instagram, X (Twitter), Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube accounts, Tumblr and Ask.fm. Many include instant messaging for private conversations, and let you add friends, including people you don't know.
Three settings to manage
Check your [[privacy settings]], tag approvals and location services on every app you use.

head: Setting
Why it matters
rows: Set them to the strongest level so only close friends can search for you, see your posts or share them.
Approve or dismiss [[tags|tag]] before they appear on your profile, so you control what you're linked to.
Some apps use your phone's location. Turn it off so people can't see where you are.
blocks.caption: Critical settings

blocks.text: Risks of social networking

items: App versions of social networks can use your **phone's location**.
Information shared between friends can be **easily copied** and spread widely.
It isn't easy to **take back** a post, and it's impossible once it's been shared.
Not everyone you meet online is **who they say they are**. Chatrooms and forums connect complete strangers and may not be moderated (checked).
Chatrooms and forums are places **online groomers** go to contact children. Some include sexual language and online flirting, sometimes over video chat.

blocks.text: Safety issues with apps

head: Safety issue
Details
rows: Meeting and chatting with strangers online risks grooming and abuse, both online and offline.
Many apps share where you are. This can put children at risk from people who want to meet them in the real world, and raises worries about identity theft and privacy.
Behind a screen, some people feel bolder about pressuring others into sending offensive or inappropriate messages and images.
blocks.caption: App safety issues

blocks.text: Snapchat's Snap Map shows friends where you are unless you turn on **Ghost Mode**. Check this setting!

blocks.title: Key points
items: Social networks let you chat, meet people and share, but most have a minimum age of 13.
Manage privacy settings, tag approvals and location services.
Posts can be copied and spread and are hard to take back.
Strangers, location sharing and pressure to send content are key app risks.

check.q: What is the minimum age for most social networking sites?
check.why: Most set 13 as the lower age limit.

check.q: Why turn off location services on social apps?
o: So people can't see where you are
check.why: Location sharing can let strangers find you.

check.q: What do tag approvals let you do?
o: Approve or dismiss tags before they appear on your profile
check.why: They give you control over what you're tagged in.

check.q: Why is it hard to take back a post?
o: Phones don't have a delete button
It may already have been copied and shared
check.why: Once shared, it's out of your control.

practice.q: Describe **three** settings you should manage on a social networking app.
practice.a: Privacy settings: restrict who sees your posts (1); tag approvals: control what you're tagged in (1); location services: stop the app showing where you are (1).

practice.q: Explain **two** risks of using social networking sites.
practice.a: e.g. Information can be copied and spread widely (1) and can't be taken back once shared (1); strangers may not be who they say they are (1) and could be groomers (1); apps may share your location (1) so people can find you (1).

pages.spec: Recognise different forms of cyberbullying and trolling
pages.summary: Cyberbullying is using electronic devices to repeatedly and deliberately harm or harass someone. It can happen 24/7 and reach huge audiences. It includes threats, harassment, defamation, exclusion, identity theft and sharing private information. Trolling is deliberately posting upsetting comments.

blocks.text: **[[Cyberbullying]]** is when someone bullies others using **electronic devices**: social media, messaging services, mobile phones, tablets or gaming platforms. The behaviour is usually **repeated** and **deliberate**. It can be horrible for the people involved and hard for them to talk about.
How is cyberbullying different?

items: It can happen **24/7**, not just at school.
It follows you **into your home**, through your phone.
It can reach a **huge audience** instantly.
It is often **anonymous**, so the victim may not know who the bully is.
It can **escalate** quickly as other people join in, so the bullying comes from many people, not just a few.

blocks.text: Forms of cyberbullying

head: Form
What it looks like
rows: Messages that try to frighten someone.
Repeatedly sending offensive, threatening or unwanted messages.
Spreading untrue rumours that damage someone's reputation.
Deliberately leaving someone out of group chats or games.
Hacking into someone's account, or making a fake one, and posting as them.
Publicly posting or forwarding private information, photos or messages about someone.
blocks.caption: Forms of cyberbullying

blocks.text: Trolling

A **troll** is a person who causes upset online by starting arguments, upsetting people or posting **inflammatory** (deliberately angering) comments. **[[Trolling]]** is often aimed at disrupting a conversation and causing distress.
Catching the bullies

Keeping **evidence** of emails, posts and messages, and telling your parents, guardians, teachers and the police, helps track down bullies. Every device online has an **IP address**, which the police and CEOP can use to trace where bullying came from, even when it's 'anonymous'.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it cyberbullying?
blocks.context: In a class group chat, a few pupils keep posting a photo of Emma with mean comments, and remove her from the chat each time she's added back.
steps: Electronic device / platform? Yes: a group chat.
Repeated? Yes: it keeps happening.
Deliberate harm? Yes: mean comments, sharing her photo and excluding her.
blocks.answer: Yes: this is cyberbullying (sharing images + exclusion). Emma should keep screenshots and tell a trusted adult.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Cyberbullying = repeated, deliberate harm using electronic devices.
It can happen 24/7, reach big audiences and be anonymous.
Forms: threats, harassment, defamation, exclusion, identity theft, sharing private information.
Trolling = deliberately posting inflammatory comments to upset people.
Keep evidence: IP addresses can be used to trace bullies.

check.q: What is cyberbullying?
o: Repeatedly and deliberately harming someone using electronic devices
check.why: That's the definition.

check.q: Someone hacks a pupil's account and posts nasty messages as them. What form of cyberbullying is this?
check.why: Posting as someone else is impersonation.

check.q: What is a troll?
o: Someone who posts inflammatory comments to cause upset
check.why: Trolls deliberately start arguments and upset people.

check.q: How can 'anonymous' cyberbullies often be traced?
check.why: IP addresses can be traced.

practice.q: Define **cyberbullying**.
practice.a: Using electronic devices/social media/messaging (1) to repeatedly and deliberately harm, harass or upset someone (1).

practice.q: Explain **two** ways cyberbullying is different from face-to-face bullying.
practice.a: Any two: it can happen 24/7 / at home (1); it can reach a large audience instantly (1); it can be anonymous (1); it can escalate quickly with many people joining in (1).

pages.spec: Recognise the warning signs of online grooming and what counts as inappropriate content
pages.summary: Online groomers pretend to be someone they're not, build trust with gifts, compliments and shared interests, then try to move to private chat, get photos or arrange to meet. Inappropriate content is anything upsetting, adult, untrue or dangerous. Never meet an online contact.

blocks.text: Online grooming

It's easy to pretend to be someone else on the internet. **[[Online grooming]]** is when someone befriends a young person and builds an **emotional connection** with them, to lower their guard so they can exploit or abuse them.
How groomers work

items: They go to apps, games and social networks used by young people and **pretend to be one of them**, often using **fake profile pictures**.
They try to gain **trust** by pretending to have the **same interests**, **offering gifts** (like game currency) and saying **nice things**.
They try to move the chat from open platforms to **private messaging**.
Once they have the child's trust, they may steer the chat towards sexual topics or **ask for photos or videos**.
Some try to **set up a meeting**, or **blackmail** the child by threatening to share pictures with their family and friends.

blocks.text: Groomers are not always strangers. Sometimes they are people already met through family or activities, who use the internet to build a closer relationship. Some young people don't realise they're being groomed and think the person is their boyfriend or girlfriend.
**Crucial rule:** adults with bad intentions can easily fake a digital identity. **Never agree to meet** an online contact in person, and never send photos to someone you don't know.
Jenny's Story: what we learn

head: Question from the class discussion
The safe answer
rows: Would you pass a stranger's contact on to a friend?
No: you'd be putting your friend at risk too.
Would you let someone from a chatroom contact you by mobile, home phone or post?
No: never give your number or address to an online contact.
Would you meet up alone with someone you only know from the internet?
Never. Not alone, and not at all without a parent's knowledge.
If you were going to meet someone, would you tell someone?
You shouldn't meet, but a trusted adult must always know about any online contact who wants to.
Do you know how to save conversations?
Yes: take screenshots, as they can be used as evidence.
If you were worried about someone who contacted you, who would you tell?
A trusted adult: parent, guardian, teacher, form tutor, Head of Year or the school's Designated Teacher for Child Protection. You can also report to CEOP.
Would you send a photo to someone you don't know?
No: once sent, you lose control of it forever.
Best advice about chatting to strangers?
Don't share personal information, don't meet up, and tell a trusted adult if anything feels wrong.
blocks.caption: Jenny's Story discussion: answers

blocks.text: Inappropriate content

What counts as **[[inappropriate content]]** differs between people and depends on age and maturity. It includes information or images that are **upsetting**, material **meant for adults**, **inaccurate** information, or anything that might lead or tempt you into **dangerous or illegal behaviour**, for example: pornography; content with swearing; sites encouraging vandalism, crime, terrorism, racism, eating disorders or self-harm; violence or cruelty to people or animals; and unsupervised chats where nobody removes unsuitable comments.
If you see something online that upsets you, close it, don't share it, and tell a trusted adult. It is never your fault.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Grooming = building an emotional connection with a young person to exploit them.
Warning signs: fake profiles, gifts, lots of compliments, moving to private chat, asking for photos or to meet.
Groomers can be strangers or people you know.
Never meet an online contact and never send photos to people you don't know.
Inappropriate content is upsetting, adult, untrue or dangerous; tell an adult if you see it.

diagram.title: How grooming can progress
diagram.caption: Spotting the early stages helps you stop it.

nodes.label: Fake friend
nodes.detail: Pretends to be a young person with a fake photo and the same interests.

nodes.label: Builds trust
nodes.detail: Compliments, gifts, game currency, always 'there for you'.

nodes.label: Goes private
nodes.detail: Asks to move to a private app, and to keep it secret.

nodes.label: Asks for more
nodes.detail: Asks for photos, or to meet. May threaten or blackmail.

nodes.label: Tell someone!
nodes.detail: At ANY stage: stop replying, keep evidence, tell a trusted adult, report to CEOP.

check.q: Which is a warning sign of online grooming?
o: Your gran comments on your photo
Someone you've never met offers you free game currency and asks to chat privately
check.why: Gifts plus moving to private chat are classic signs.

check.q: Are online groomers always strangers?
o: No, they can be people the child already knows
check.why: Groomers may already know the child.

check.q: Someone you met in a game asks to meet you in Enniskillen on Saturday. What should you do?
o: Don't go, and tell a trusted adult
Ask them for a photo first
check.why: Never meet; tell an adult.

check.q: Which of these is inappropriate content?
check.why: Content encouraging harmful behaviour is inappropriate.

practice.q: Describe **three** ways an online groomer might try to gain a young person's trust.
practice.a: Any three: pretending to be a young person / fake profile picture (1); pretending to share their interests (1); offering gifts or game currency (1); saying nice things/compliments (1).

practice.q: Give **two** examples of inappropriate content.
practice.a: Any two: pornography (1); content with swearing (1); sites encouraging crime/vandalism/terrorism/racism/eating disorders/self-harm (1); violence or cruelty to people or animals (1); inaccurate information (1).

pages.spec: Explain what a digital footprint and a digital reputation are, and how quickly a post can spread
pages.summary: Your digital footprint is the often permanent trail left by everything you do online. Your digital reputation is how people see you because of it, and it can affect friendships and future jobs. A post can reach millions through friends of friends, so stop and THINK before you post.

blocks.text: Your digital footprint

Your **[[digital footprint]]** is *"the trail or history left behind by all your interactions using the internet, email, social media, texting, instant messaging and even on-demand TV."* It can often be **permanent**. Once something has been sent, you lose control over it.
Footprints in the sand: how far can a post spread?

blocks.title: Worked example: how many people could see your post?
blocks.context: You post a photo. You have 200 online friends, and each person has about 500 friends of their own.
steps: Your friends: **200** people can see it.
Friends of friends: 200 × 500 = **100,000** people.
Friends of friends of friends: 100,000 × 500 = **50,000,000** people.
blocks.answer: Up to 50 million people: that's over 25 times the population of Northern Ireland (about 1.9 million)!

blocks.text: Real numbers are smaller because friend groups overlap, but the point stands: a post can spread far beyond the people you meant it for.
Your digital reputation

Your **[[digital reputation]]** is defined by your **behaviour online** and by the **content you post** about yourself and others. Tagged photos, blog posts and social media interactions all shape how people see you, online and offline, now and in the future.
A poor digital reputation can affect your **friendships**, **relationships** and even your **job prospects**. Many employers and universities look people up online.
**THINK** before you post. Is it **T**rue? Is it **H**elpful? Is it **I**nspiring? Is it **N**ecessary? Is it **K**ind?
Some guidelines to remember

items: Never post pictures online that reveal personal details.
Never post personal information online.
Never post unacceptable comments online.
Keep your profile private.
Only accept real friends as your online friends.
Use an avatar as your profile picture.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Digital footprint = the trail left by everything you do online; often permanent.
One post can spread to millions through friends of friends.
Digital reputation = how others see you from your online behaviour and posts.
A poor reputation can affect friendships and job prospects, so stop and THINK before you post.

diagram.title: How far could my post spread?
diagram.caption: Change the number of friends to see how many friends-of-friends-of-friends (each with 500 friends) could see a post.

check.q: What is a digital footprint?
o: The trail of information left by everything you do online
check.why: It's your online trail.

check.q: You have 100 friends and each has 500 friends. How many 'friends of friends' could see your post?
What can a poor digital reputation affect?
check.why: It can affect your future.

check.q: What does the T in THINK stand for?
check.why: Is it True?

practice.q: Explain the difference between a digital footprint and a digital reputation.
practice.a: A digital footprint is the trail/history of everything you do online (1); a digital reputation is how others see/judge you based on that behaviour and content (1).

practice.q: Explain why something you post online could affect you in the future.
practice.a: Posts can be permanent / copied and shared, so they can't be taken back (1); employers or others may see them later and judge you, affecting job prospects (1).

pages.spec: Know exactly what to do if something online makes you uncomfortable, and nine tips for staying safe
pages.summary: If anything online makes you uncomfortable: don't delete it (it's evidence), don't reply, tell a trusted adult and report it to CEOP or Childline. Stay safe by using strong privacy settings, blocking and reporting, keeping personal details private and only friending people you know.

blocks.text: Feeling uncomfortable online? Do this
Saved messages and screenshots are [[evidence]]. Follow these four steps:

head: Step
Why
rows: Keep messages, images, emails and screenshots. They are **evidence** that police and school can use, for example to trace IP addresses, even if it goes to court.
Replying to bullies or trolls makes things worse and can make an investigation harder.
A parent, guardian, grandparent, form tutor, Head of Year, the school's Designated Teacher for Child Protection, or any teacher.
Use the **[[CEOP]]** reporting button (Child Exploitation and Online Protection) or contact **[[Childline]]** on **0800 1111**. You can also report on the app or game itself.
blocks.caption: What to do if something online worries you

blocks.text: If you think someone is in **immediate danger**, call **999**. CEOP is the place to report anyone trying to meet up with a child or acting in a sexual way online.
Nine tips for staying safe online

items: **Educate yourself** about what the social networks and apps you use actually do.
Set up **privacy settings** at the strongest level.
**Report** people and inappropriate conversations using the 'report' button, and always **keep a copy** as evidence.
**[[Block]]** or ignore people on social networks and games who make you feel uncomfortable.
**Never share personal details**: passwords, real name, address or school name.
**Friends should be people you know.** People online may not be who they say they are. Never agree to meet someone you don't know.
Know what you **should and shouldn't post** online.
Report directly to **CEOP** if someone is trying to meet up with a young person, or if someone is in immediate danger.
Remember that what you post **can't always be taken back**, and may already have been shared. This applies to **webcams** too.

blocks.title: Worked example: what should Niamh do?
blocks.context: Niamh keeps getting nasty anonymous messages on a social app saying nobody likes her.
steps: Don't delete: screenshot every message with the date and time.
Don't reply to the sender.
Block and report the account on the app.
Tell a trusted adult (a parent, her form tutor or Head of Year).
If it continues or she feels unsafe, the adult can involve the police; she can also talk to Childline on 0800 1111.
blocks.answer: Save, don't reply, block and report, tell an adult.

blocks.text: Don't just block and delete everything straight away. Save the evidence first!

blocks.title: Key points
items: Don't delete messages: they are evidence.
Don't reply to bullies or strangers.
Tell a trusted adult immediately.
Report to CEOP or call Childline on 0800 1111.
Use strong privacy settings, block and report, and never share personal details or meet online contacts.

nodes.label: Something worries you
nodes.detail: A message, image or person online makes you feel uncomfortable.

nodes.label: Don't delete
nodes.detail: Keep messages and screenshots as evidence.

nodes.label: Tell an adult
nodes.detail: Parent, guardian, form tutor, Head of Year or any teacher.

nodes.label: Report
nodes.detail: CEOP reporting button or Childline on 0800 1111.

check.q: Why should you NOT delete upsetting messages?
o: They can be used as evidence
check.why: Messages are evidence.

check.q: What is Childline's phone number?
check.why: Childline is 0800 1111.

check.q: What does CEOP stand for?
check.why: CEOP = Child Exploitation and Online Protection.

check.q: Someone sends you threatening messages. What should you NOT do?
o: Reply with threats of your own
check.why: Never reply or retaliate.

practice.q: Describe the **four** steps you should take if someone online makes you feel uncomfortable.
practice.a: Don't delete the messages / keep them as evidence (1); don't reply (1); tell a trusted adult such as a parent or teacher (1); report it to CEOP or Childline (1).

practice.q: State **four** tips you would give a friend to help them stay safe online.
practice.a: Any four: strongest privacy settings (1); report and keep evidence (1); block people who make you uncomfortable (1); never share personal details (1); only friend people you know / never meet online contacts (1); think about what you post (1); learn what apps do (1); report to CEOP (1); posts can't be taken back (1).

pages.spec: Plan, organise and evaluate a team e-safety video project
pages.summary: In a team of three you plan, create and edit a video of up to 2 minutes promoting online safety. You share out roles, organise assets in folders, respect copyright, export the finished video and then use feedback to evaluate and improve it.

blocks.text: To finish the topic, you work in a **team of three** to plan, design, create and edit a video, **no longer than 2 minutes**, promoting **staying safe online**. It takes about three lessons, plus home learning.
Skills you'll need

head: Skill
What it means in the project
rows: Talking and listening so everyone knows the plan.
Files saved in the right folders, deadlines met.
Doing your fair share and helping others.
The video teaches real e-safety facts.
An original, eye-catching way to get the message across.
blocks.caption: Project skills

blocks.text: Team roles

head: Role
Who
Job
rows: Finds the facts and gathers suitable images.
Plans the storyboard and the look of the video.
Builds the project in a video editor (e.g. Clipchamp, Canva or MovieMaker).
Adds transitions, audio, effects and checks timing.
Keeps the team on track and files organised.
blocks.caption: Five roles shared between three people

blocks.text: Organising it all

You've already been file-management wizards, so now prove it! Create a folder called **E SAFETY** in your *Year 8 > ICT* folder, with subfolders **Images**, **Video Assets** and **Audio**. Give **everything** a meaningful name, and don't leave e-safety images in 'My Pictures'. If you record clips at home, bring them in on a USB stick or in Google Drive.

Respect **[[copyright]]**. Don't rip music or videos from YouTube with converter websites: it breaks YouTube's rules and can break copyright law, and those sites are full of pop-ups and malware. Use your own footage, **[[royalty-free]]** music and images, or school-approved libraries, and credit the owner.
Finishing and presenting

items: Check for transitions, audio, effects, timing, spelling, clarity and accurate information, and test that it plays.
**Export** the finished video in a suitable format such as **MP4** (or WMV), not the project file.
Name it with everyone's names, e.g. *ONLINE SAFETY VIDEO – BY MR BUTLER.mp4*.
Prepare notes for presenting it to the class. Classmates rate each video: two great things, one possible improvement, does it get the e-safety message across, and a score out of 10.

blocks.text: Feedback and evaluation

**[[Feedback]]** and **[[evaluation]]** matter because they let you judge the **progress** you've made, see your **strengths** and **areas for development**, recognise **what you've learnt** that you can use in future, and decide what **improvements** to make next time.

When you evaluate your video, take in comments from the class, your teacher, your group and your own view. Ask: Do all images, audio and video work? Is the message consistent? Is the look and feel consistent? Are the effects and transitions consistent? Is the narration good? A good evaluation is both **positive** and **critical**, e.g. *"I liked our colour scheme, but next time I'd keep all the text boxes the same style."*

blocks.title: Key points
items: Teams of three make a video (max 2 minutes) promoting online safety.
Roles: researcher, designer, creator, editor, organiser.
Organise assets in E SAFETY > Images, Video Assets, Audio, with meaningful names.
Respect copyright: use your own or royalty-free media and credit owners.
Export the final video (e.g. MP4) and use feedback to evaluate and improve.

check.q: What is the maximum length of the e-safety video?
check.why: No longer than 2 minutes.

check.q: What should you submit at the end?
o: The exported video, e.g. an MP4
check.why: Submit the exported video, not the project file.

check.q: Why is feedback and evaluation important?
o: It lets you judge progress and plan improvements
check.why: It shows strengths, weaknesses and next steps.

check.q: Which is the safest way to get music for your video?
o: Rip it from YouTube with a converter site
Use royalty-free music and credit it
check.why: Royalty-free music respects copyright.

practice.q: Give **three** reasons why feedback and evaluation are important.
practice.a: Any three: lets you judge the progress you've made (1); shows strengths and areas for development (1); shows what you've learnt that you can apply to future work (1); helps you decide improvements for future projects (1).

practice.q: Explain why you should organise your project files into folders with meaningful names.
practice.a: So everyone in the team can find files quickly / nothing gets lost (1), and you don't waste time or save duplicates (1).

glossary.def: The safe and responsible use of technology, including the internet, phones, gaming devices and email.
Keeping control over your personal information and who can see it.
Someone who uses the internet safely, responsibly and respectfully towards others.
Information that could identify you or be used to find you, such as your full name, address, phone number or school.
Adding your exact location to a photo or post, often done automatically by your phone.
A picture or cartoon character used to represent you online instead of a real photo.
Options on an app or website that control who can see your posts and profile and who can contact you.
Playing games over the internet in real time with other people around the world.
Deliberately spoiling other players' game, for example by harassing them or cheating; a form of bullying.
Spending real money inside a game on extras such as skins, items or game currency.
Short for malicious software: any program designed to harm a computer or steal data, such as viruses, trojans, worms and spyware.
Malware disguised as genuine, useful software, such as a free game mod, that secretly lets attackers in.
Malware that spreads itself across a network from computer to computer without needing to attach to a file.
Software secretly installed to watch what you do and steal information such as passwords; a keylogger records every key you press.
Fake emails or messages pretending to be from a real organisation, such as a bank, to trick you into giving away personal details.
Secretly redirecting you from a real website to a fake copy to steal your login details.
The legal right of the creator to control who can copy, share or sell their work, such as music, films and software.
Using websites and apps such as Instagram, Snapchat or TikTok to share posts and messages and keep in touch with people.
Labelling a person in a photo or post, which links it to their profile.
A phone setting that lets apps know where you are using GPS.
Using electronic devices, such as phones, social media or gaming platforms, to repeatedly and deliberately harm or harass someone.
Deliberately posting offensive or provocative comments online to start arguments or upset people.
Spreading untrue things about someone that damage their reputation.
Pretending to be someone else, for example by hacking their account and posting as them.
When someone builds a friendship and emotional connection with a young person online in order to trick, exploit or abuse them.
Material that is upsetting, meant for adults, untrue, or that could lead you into dangerous or illegal behaviour.
The trail of information you leave behind from everything you do online; it is often permanent.
How others see you, based on your behaviour online and what you and others post about you.
Child Exploitation and Online Protection: part of the UK's National Crime Agency, where young people can report online abuse or worrying contact.
A free, confidential helpline for children and young people, on 0800 1111 or online.
Proof of what happened, such as saved messages or screenshots, that can be used by school or police.
To stop a person contacting you or seeing your profile on an app or game.
Looking back at your work to judge its strengths and weaknesses and decide how to improve it.
Comments from others, such as your teacher or classmates, about what is good in your work and what could be better.
Media (images, music, video) you are allowed to use without paying each time, as long as you follow its licence.
